clips.send: A tradesman's kid stuck clocking in sends this to a cousin thinking about starting a business - the realization that every house in the rich neighborhood belonged to an owner, never a worker, with a flash of anger at the years of apprenticeship it used to cost just to get in.
clips.caption:
Kevin Trudeau grew up in a 1,200-square-foot house with one bathroom. His dad was a welder. Every neighbor was a tradesman - electrician, bricklayer, mason, carpenter, butcher.

Then he drove through the rich part of town and asked his father what those people did. Nobody was a worker. Every single one owned a business - the dry cleaner, the glass company, the car dealership, the restaurant chain.

Back then the only way in was years as an apprentice, learning someone else's business with no guarantee you'd ever go out on your own.

That's the price people used to pay to stop trading hours for a paycheck.

What's stopping you from paying it today?
